metric.why: Rates rising after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply. Rate data is compiled by commercial research firms listed in the directory below; it is not republished here.
metric.definition: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.

reading.body:
Colocation rental rates rising after a decade of decline signal that AI demand for data center capacity now exceeds available supply in major markets.

A decade of falling rates meant data center operators competed on price while demand remained stable. The reversal of this trend is a market price signal: scarcity. When the cost per kilowatt climbs despite new construction, it means new buildings and power connections are not keeping pace with what compute demands require. This is the clearest evidence available that the constraint has shifted from having too much capacity to having too little.

For AI scaling, rising rental rates matter because they compress margins for every company dependent on leased infrastructure. Hyperscalers building their own facilities can absorb higher power costs more easily than smaller operators renting colocation space. The rate climb also indicates that even where buildings exist, the power to fill them is the limiting factor. A data center cannot rent what it cannot power.

This metric does not tell you which geographies are most constrained, how long current rate levels will hold, or whether planned power and construction projects will reverse the trend. It shows only that demand has outrun supply in aggregate. To understand where AI capacity will actually flow, you need to look at power infrastructure timelines and regional building pipelines separately.
